overview: Barotse refers here to the Lozi kingdom and its many communities around the upper Zambezi floodplain in western Zambia. The imported 1878 to 1914 window covers a late phase of royal and colonial history. Its polygon lies mainly north of the floodplain heartland described below and should not be treated as a verified kingdom boundary.

periods.title: Lewanika and the royal landscape
periods.summary: Lewanika first ruled in 1878, was briefly deposed in 1884 and returned in 1885. Royal building and canals reshaped the floodplain.

periods.title: Colonial agreements and continuing royal authority
periods.summary: Protectorate arrangements in 1890 and 1900 changed the kingdom’s political position. The map’s 1914 cutoff is not the disappearance of the Lozi.

sections.title: Living with a river that changes its address

items.text: Families raised earth into settlement mounds above the surrounding plain. Seasonal flooding still required movement to higher ground. The Kuomboka journey carries the Litunga from Lealui toward Limulunga; other households also relocate. Moving season follows the river’s timetable.

The Mwayowamo canal, dated 1887 to 1889 in Zambia’s heritage account, connected Lealui and Limulunga and supplied Lealui with water. Other channels drained fields or carried boats. These were useful engineering works with several jobs, rather than a decorative moat around a palace.

Fishers built malelo weirs to retain water as floods receded. Opening a gap let water pass into a waiting basket and helped catch fish. Temporary maongo shelters of reeds, grass or branches served people at fishing camps and during seasonal moves.

sections.title: A table with ducks and baskets with animals

items.text: A wooden food bowl now in the British Museum has six swimming ducks carved on its lid. Dated about 1891 to 1901, it carried a collector’s label saying it was used by headmen. A remarkable serving dish, but not a census of everyone’s dinnerware.

Court objects drew on different communities’ skills. The museum identifies Kwangwa and Mbunda carvers among those meeting demand for wooden vessels at the Lozi court. The kingdom’s artistic achievements belonged to people with distinct identities, not to one ruler working alone.

Women made tightly coiled baskets for storing valuable goods. A surviving example from about 1900 to 1920 uses Makenge root fibre and pigment. Its orderly woven surface turns a flexible plant material into a carefully shaped, lidded container.

Overseas demand changed basket decoration during Lewanika’s reign. The Metropolitan Museum contrasts earlier geometric designs with animal figures made for European customers. On this basket, figures march around lid and body: a procession you could carry under your arm.

The canal-building story also includes coercion. Historian Jack Hogan’s archival research identifies enslaved labour as central to major royal public works. Admiring the engineering should leave room for the workers whose effort was demanded rather than freely offered.

Slavery was formally abolished in 1906, but Hogan follows its slow decline over the next two decades. A proclamation did not instantly free every person from a master’s control. The difference between a law and everyday freedom is part of the kingdom’s history.

Barotse National School opened in March 1907 with seven pupils, according to the education history summarized by Peggy Mwanza. An agreement with Lewanika allocated a share of local tax revenue to education. The tiny opening class belonged to a much larger argument about who should fund schooling.

sections.title: A living language and later everyday life

items.text: “Bà-shímànì bà-ká-sèh-à” means “The boys will laugh.” This Silozi example was published by linguists in 2025 from work with speaker Mubiana Liswaniso in 2022 to 2024. The Latin letters, tone marks and hyphens reproduce their notation. It is a modern language witness, not a royal document from 1878.

A 2015 canals report describes a continuing practical problem: sandy ground and scarce building stone made durable latrines difficult. It also records boreholes serving schools and health centres. These are dated modern observations, showing why water management includes safe drinking water and sanitation as well as boat routes.

ending.text: Colonial agreements gradually reduced independent royal power; 1914 is only this map record’s endpoint. In 1964 a new agreement addressed Barotseland’s place within independent Zambia and replaced earlier British obligations. That political change did not end Lozi communities or royal traditions. The parliamentary explanation records the settlement’s intended framework, not a guarantee that every later dispute was resolved.
